name: Campaign Legal Center (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends and reforms; the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: The Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal organisation in Washington (its 501(c)(4), Campaign Legal Center Action, is left out: gifts to it aren't tax-deductible), spent $21.5 million in 2025 on litigation and advocacy for voting rights, fair maps, campaign finance law and ethics, and against the administration's executive order on elections. Two branches: its direct work against a slide (about a third of its spending), 0.29% of the US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030 (the shared 11%, cut by about a twentieth), valued by the income a slide would cost as it builds up (nearly half of the result); and the rest, its voting-rights, redistricting, campaign-finance and ethics work, counted as reform work only at the site's shared figures for reforms within a democracy. With its next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average (it holds about 19 months of spending available), it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The result is mostly judgment (the years a win counts, the field's effect on the breakdown risk, how much a reform dollar does against a redistricting dollar, the split of its spending between the branches), and both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: The Campaign Legal Center's own spending in calendar 2025 on its seven program columns, with its administrative and fundraising costs, from the audited statement of functional expenses. Campaign Legal Center Action, the 501(c)(4), is left out: gifts to it aren't tax-deductible. Every program is democracy work, split between direct work against a slide and reform work (voting rights, redistricting, campaign finance, ethics), valued in the reform branch alone.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Who the work reaches: everyone governed by US democracy (the slide branch), and the people a reform of the redistricting movement's size reaches each year (the reform branch's yardstick).

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the work changes: the chance that US democracy slides to a hybrid regime, valued by the income a slide would cost as it builds up; and reforms within the democracy, valued at the shared figures for the redistricting movement scaled by the relative effect of other reforms. Each counts the whole field's or movement's effect; the Center's share is in the adjustments.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's own discounts for trust in the estimate, the Campaign Legal Center's share of its field's resources, delivery and missing data; the canonical rows are their averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.explainer: Administrative ($3.9 million) and fundraising ($1.6 million) spread over the programs.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programmes, including overhead
rows.explainer: The whole year's spending, $21.5 million: every program is democracy work, so the branches below split all of it.

rows.label: Share of Voting Rights acting on a slide directly
rows.explainer: About half: the lawsuits against the executive order on elections and against the use of states' voter files, the naturalization-ceremony case and the separation-of-powers briefs act on a slide directly (the field's 'direct' dollar: litigation and checks on executive power, @democracy.field_direct_share); voting-rights cases under the Voting Rights Act, Restore Your Vote and state policy work are reforms within a democracy. Judged 50% (30% to 70%), from the annual report's account of 2025 (pp. 4 and 11), whose lead items are the direct ones.

rows.label: Share of Ethics acting on a slide directly
rows.explainer: Complaints against administration officials' conflicts of interest and the defence of independent ethics enforcement hold power to account (direct); complaints against members of Congress and the stock-trading ban are ethics reform. Judged 30% (10% to 50%).

rows.label: Share of Redistricting acting on a slide directly
rows.explainer: Fair-maps litigation is reform work within a democracy (the redistricting and other-reform chain); the suit against Missouri's map drawn under the administration's pressure for a mid-decade redistricting is closer to checks on power, and the annual report frames the 2025 redistricting work as a fight against that multistate campaign to keep a House majority (p. 8), which is why the high end is 35%. Judged 15% (0 to 35%).

rows.label: Share of Campaign Finance acting on a slide directly
rows.explainer: Money-in-politics enforcement and defence of limits are reform work (@democracy.other_reform_relative_effect names money in politics); the briefs on the president's power over the Federal Election Commission are the small direct part. Judged 5% (0 to 15%).

rows.label: Share of Other Programs acting on a slide directly
rows.explainer: Undescribed in the accounts, but the donor-restricted release for the anti-sabotage project (protecting the certification of elections, direct work), $1,183,535 in 2025 (note 8), is two thirds of the column, against $50,000 for the Charles Fried Fellowship; the rest may be Restore Your Vote and other reform work. Judged 60% (30% to 80%).

rows.label: Share of the programme acting on a slide directly
rows.formula: (vot_fy2025 * vot_direct_share + eth_fy2025 * eth_direct_share + red_fy2025 * red_direct_share + cfi_fy2025 * cfi_direct_share + oth_fy2025 * oth_direct_share) / (vot_fy2025 + eth_fy2025 + red_fy2025 + cfi_fy2025 + oth_fy2025)
rows.explainer: The five program columns' direct shares weighted by their spending (about 35%); Communications and Policy work across the teams and follow the same split. The rest is reform work, valued in the reform branch alone and never also against a slide (the family's rule).

rows.label: Long-run income gain from staying a democracy (share of GDP per person)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Acemoglu et al. 2019): about a fifth of income per person, what a coded reversal out of democracy costs in the long run (p. 76: reversals have effects similar to democratizations).

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a slide to a hybrid regime would lose
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json), read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Long-run income loss of a slide per person per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + gain × severity): the full long-run loss on the shared log scale, valued at $uov_per_ln_consumption; its build-up is in dem_loss_years.

rows.label: Chance the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030
rows.explainer: The shared forecast (about {{row:dem_p_breakdown}}, 5% to 28%): the stake the democracy work acts on. A cut in a chance is counted at its expected value, as the catastrophic-risk models count a cut in a hazard: the field's work is thousands of cases and campaigns, not one bet, so it isn't a single event.

rows.label: Relative cut in that chance from one year of the whole US pro-democracy field's work
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json), read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Chance a year of the field's work averts a slide
rows.explainer: Breakdown risk × the field's relative cut; the Campaign Legal Center's share of the field is in dem_attribution_share.

rows.label: Years from the work until a slide it averts would have come
rows.explainer: The shared slide-date window (the Economist's reports before 2030; those for 2024 and 2025 showed no slide, so 2026 to 2028, on average 2027), measured from calendar 2025's work: 2 years (1 to 4).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Chance per year that a slide, once it happens, is reversed
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json), read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Rate for the slide's loss: the shared discount rate plus the reversal hazard
rows.explainer: The loss averted lasts only while the slide would have lasted.

rows.label: Years over which a slide's income loss builds up
rows.explainer: The shared figure (about 25 years, 20 to 30).

rows.label: Discounted years of the full loss averted by putting a slide off
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + dem_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + dem_rate) ^ (0 - dem_ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + dem_rate) * ln(1 + dem_rate) * dem_ramp_years) * dem_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The family's shifted ramp: a slide's loss builds evenly over dem_ramp_years; putting the slide off by the years counted ($win_years_counted) moves the whole ramp later, so the loss avoided rises to a fifth of the full loss over the first five years, stays there until the ramp is complete and falls back to nothing five years later, years_of_impact full-loss years in all before discounting. Its present value (continuous form) at dem_rate, times the wait at the shared rate: about {{row:dem_loss_years}} full-loss years at the defaults.
